title: Cross-Validation & Model Selection
blurb: Tests how to get an honest performance estimate: fold arithmetic, stratification, time-ordered and grouped splits, leakage through preprocessing, nested CV and fair model comparison.

ideas.title: Single-split variance and test-set selection bias

refLinks.label: §13.2.1 The Problem With a Single Train/Test Split

ideas.title: Preprocessing leakage and the Pipeline pattern
Nested CV and the cost of a search

questions.prompt: A team trains 50 models, scores each on the same test set, and reports the best score as the performance of the chosen model. Why is that number optimistic?
options: Each extra evaluation retrains the model on part of the test set, so later scores see the answers
Scoring 50 models wears the test set out, so each later score is computed on fewer examples
The winning model has overfitted its training data, so it is secretly worse than the other 49
Picking the maximum of 50 noisy scores favours whichever model got lucky on that test set
questions.explanation: Every test score is the true performance plus noise from which examples landed in the test set. Picking the maximum of 50 such numbers picks the model with the most favourable noise. The chapter stresses that the winner is not secretly worse. The *selection process* is what inflates the number. Scoring a fixed model does not retrain it or consume the test set.

questions.prompt: In plain 5-fold cross-validation, how often does each example sit in a validation fold, and in how many of the five training sets does it appear?
options: It depends on the seed, and some examples may never be validated
Five times in a validation fold, and in one of the five training sets
Once in a validation fold, and in one of the five training sets
Once in a validation fold, and in four of the five training sets
questions.explanation: The data is cut into 5 disjoint folds. Each round holds one fold out and trains on the other four. Over 5 rounds each example is validated exactly once and used for training in the other 4 rounds. The folds are a partition, so no example is skipped, whatever the seed.

questions.prompt: What does `StratifiedKFold` guarantee that plain `KFold` does not?
options: Each fold holds an equal number of examples from every class
Rows from the same group never appear in both training and validation
Each fold keeps about the same class proportions as the full dataset
Rows keep their original time order, so validation is always later
questions.explanation: Stratification preserves the class *ratio*. With 5% positives, every fold gets about 5% positives. It does not rebalance to equal counts per class. Time order is `TimeSeriesSplit`'s job, and keeping groups together is `GroupKFold`'s job.

questions.prompt: With default settings, which statement about scikit-learn's `TimeSeriesSplit` is correct?
options: Rows are shuffled within each month, then whole months are assigned to folds at random
Each split uses a fixed-size training window that slides forward, dropping the oldest rows
Each validation block comes later than its training rows, and training windows grow
The most recent block is held out once, and the same split is repeated k times with new seeds
questions.explanation: `TimeSeriesSplit` never shuffles. Split $i$ trains on everything before its validation block, so training windows expand while validation stays strictly ahead. A sliding window is possible only if you set `max_train_size`, which is not the default.

questions.prompt: A notebook runs `X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)` and then `cross_val_score(model, X_scaled, y, cv=5)`. What is wrong?
options: The scaler must be fitted on each validation fold and then applied to the matching training folds instead
Scaler statistics came from rows later used for validation, so validation data leaked into training
Nothing is wrong, because a scaler never looks at `y` and so it cannot leak anything
Scaling must happen after the model is fitted, otherwise the learned coefficients end up on the wrong scale
questions.explanation: Any fitted preprocessing step learns statistics from the data it sees. Fitting on all of `X` means each validation fold has shaped the mean and std used to transform the training folds. The leak does not need the labels. Leakage is about validation data influencing training, and the fix is to put the scaler inside a `Pipeline` so it is refitted on each training split.

questions.prompt: In nested cross-validation, what do the two loops do?
options: Inner picks hyperparameters within each outer training set, outer scores the result on unseen data
The inner loop estimates generalisation performance, and the outer loop picks the hyperparameters to ship
Both loops tune hyperparameters, and the outer loop averages the chosen values into one setting
The inner loop trains the final production model, and the outer loop decides which features to keep
questions.explanation: Nested CV separates selection from evaluation. The inner search (for example 3-fold `GridSearchCV`) runs inside each outer training set. The outer fold it is then scored on was never used for selection, so the outer average is an honest estimate of the whole tune-then-train procedure. The outer loop does not choose the model to ship.

questions.prompt: Listing 13.5 compares two models with `stats.ttest_rel` on their 10 fold scores. Why a *paired* test?
options: A paired test assumes the two models' scores are independent, which cross-validation guarantees
Paired tests need fewer folds than unpaired tests, so they are cheaper to compute on large data
Both models see the same folds, so testing per-fold differences cancels shared fold difficulty
An unpaired test would require each model to be scored with a different metric on each fold
questions.explanation: Fold 3 may be hard for every model and fold 7 easy. Those shared swings inflate the spread of each model's scores. Pairing by fold tests the differences $a_i - b_i$, which removes the shared fold effect. Paired scores are *not* independent. That dependence is the reason to pair them.

questions.prompt: A model's true accuracy is 0.90. It is scored on a random test set of 120 examples. Using the binomial standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, what is the standard error of the measured accuracy? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{0.90 \times 0.10}{120}} = \sqrt{0.00075} \approx 0.0274$$
Two standard errors either side covers roughly 0.845 to 0.955. A single split can report anything in that range for the same model, which is the chapter's point about 91% versus 97%.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 1,200 rows. You run `KFold(n_splits=8)`. How many rows are in each training set? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Each fold holds $1200/8 = 150$ rows. Each round trains on the other 7 folds, so $7 \times 150 = 1050$ rows. A common slip is to answer 150, which is the validation size.

questions.prompt: A 5-fold run returns `scores = np.array([0.84, 0.88, 0.86, 0.90, 0.82])`. Listing 13.1 prints `scores.std()`, which uses NumPy's default `ddof=0`. What value does it print? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
Mean $= 4.30/5 = 0.86$. Deviations are $-0.02, 0.02, 0, 0.04, -0.04$. Squares sum to $0.0004+0.0004+0+0.0016+0.0016 = 0.0040$.
$$\sigma = \sqrt{0.0040/5} = \sqrt{0.0008} \approx 0.0283$$
Dividing by $n-1=4$ instead (sample std) gives 0.0316. NumPy's `.std()` divides by $n$ unless you pass `ddof=1`.

questions.prompt: A fraud dataset has 1,000 rows and 60 of them are positive. You run `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5)`. How many positives are in each *training* set? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Stratification puts $60/5 = 12$ positives in each validation fold. Each training set is the other four folds, so it holds $4 \times 12 = 48$ positives out of 800 rows, still 6%.

questions.prompt: You apply `TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)` with default settings to 600 time-ordered rows. scikit-learn makes each validation block $\lfloor 600/(5+1) \rfloor = 100$ rows, and each training set is every row before its validation block. How many rows are in the training set of the *third* split? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: The first 100 rows are only ever used for training. Split 1 trains on rows 0 to 99 and validates on 100 to 199. Split 2 trains on 200 rows, and split 3 trains on rows 0 to 299, so 300 rows, then validates on rows 300 to 399. The last split trains on 500. This is the table's weakness: early splits train on much less data.

questions.prompt: Which of these gives a leakage-free 5-fold accuracy estimate for a scaled SVM with feature selection?
options: `Xk = SelectKBest(k=10).fit_transform(X, y)`, then `cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()), Xk, y, cv=5)`
`Xs = StandardScaler().fit(X[:100]).transform(X)`, then `cross_val_score(make_pipeline(SelectKBest(k=10), SVC()), Xs, y, cv=5)`
`Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)`, then `cross_val_score(make_pipeline(SelectKBest(k=10), SVC()), Xs, y, cv=5)`
`cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(k=10), SVC()), X, y, cv=5)`
questions.explanation: Only the first option refits *every* fitted step on each training split. The second fits the scaler on all rows. The third is the worst: `SelectKBest` looked at every label, validation labels included, before CV started. The fourth fits the scaler on 100 rows that will also appear in validation folds.

questions.prompt: `GridSearchCV` searches a grid of 4 values of `C` and 3 values of `gamma`, with `cv=5` and the default `refit=True`. How many times is the model fitted when you call `search.fit(X, y)`? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: There are $4 \times 3 = 12$ combinations. Each is fitted once per fold: $12 \times 5 = 60$. With `refit=True` the best combination is refitted once more on all of `X`, giving 61.

questions.prompt: Across 10 folds a model's scores have a standard deviation of 0.020. Estimate the standard error of the mean CV score as $\text{std}/\sqrt{k}$. Give a decimal to 4 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$$\text{SE} = 0.020/\sqrt{10} = 0.020/3.162 \approx 0.0063$$
The fold std describes how much one fold's score varies. The SE describes how precisely the *mean* is known. A 0.3 percentage-point gap between two such models is about half an SE, which is why Procedure 13.5 warns it can easily be noise. (Folds share training data, so this SE is a rough guide, not exact.)

questions.prompt: Twenty candidate models all have the same true accuracy, 0.80. Each is scored on a 100-example test set. Treat each measured score as normal with standard error 0.04 and, for simplicity, independent across models. For one model, $P(\text{score} \ge 0.88) = P(Z \ge 2) \approx 0.0228$. What is the probability that the *best* of the 20 scores is at least 0.88? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
The best score is below 0.88 only if all 20 are below it.
$$P(\max \ge 0.88) = 1 - (1 - 0.0228)^{20} = 1 - 0.9772^{20} \approx 1 - 0.631 = 0.369$$
So more than a third of the time the reported winner shows 88% or more although every model is truly 80%. That is selection bias. On a shared test set the scores are correlated, which shrinks the effect somewhat, but it does not remove it.

questions.prompt: You run leave-one-out CV on 40 rows. The model gets 37 of the 40 held-out points right. Each fold's score is 1 (correct) or 0 (wrong). What is the standard deviation (`ddof=0`) of the 40 fold scores? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
Mean accuracy $p = 37/40 = 0.925$. For 0/1 scores the population std is $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$.
$$\sqrt{0.925 \times 0.075} = \sqrt{0.069375} \approx 0.263$$
The mean is fine, but the per-fold spread is huge because each fold is one right-or-wrong outcome. That is the "high variance between folds" in the Trade-offs table. It says nothing about model instability.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 100 rows and only 5 positives. You use plain `KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True)`, so the first validation fold is a random 20 of the 100 rows. What is the probability that this fold contains *no* positives? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
This is hypergeometric: choose all 20 rows from the 95 negatives.
$$P = \frac{\binom{95}{20}}{\binom{100}{20}} = \frac{80 \cdot 79 \cdot 78 \cdot 77 \cdot 76}{100 \cdot 99 \cdot 98 \cdot 97 \cdot 96} \approx 0.319$$
About one fold in three has no positives at all, so recall or F1 cannot even be computed there. `StratifiedKFold` puts exactly one positive in each fold.

questions.prompt: A hospital has 3,000 chest X-rays from 600 patients, about five per patient. Shuffled `StratifiedKFold` reports AUC 0.96. On a batch of new patients the model scores 0.81. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scans were taken over time, so shuffling leaked the future. Use `TimeSeriesSplit` ordered on scan date
Five folds are too few for 3,000 images. Use `LeaveOneOut` to use as much training data as possible
Each patient's images sit in both training and validation. Use `GroupKFold` grouped by patient ID
The folds lost the class balance during shuffling. Use `StratifiedKFold` with `n_splits=10` to tighten the class ratio
questions.explanation: Several rows per patient means validation images have near-copies (same patient) in training. CV then measures recall of known patients, not generalisation to new ones. The Quick Reference fix is `GroupKFold`, which keeps every patient on one side. Stratification was already on, and nothing in the scenario says time order drives the target. LOOCV would make the patient leak worse.

questions.prompt: In one CV round, the training fold's values for a feature are $[2, 4, 6, 8]$ and the validation fold holds one row with value 20. A correct `Pipeline` fits `StandardScaler` (population std) on the training fold only. What scaled value does the validation row receive? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
Training mean $= 5$. Population variance $= (9+1+1+9)/4 = 5$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$.
$$z = (20 - 5)/2.236 \approx 6.71$$
If the scaler were fitted on all five values (the leak), the mean is 8 and $\sigma = \sqrt{200/5} \approx 6.32$, giving $z \approx 1.90$. The leak makes an extreme validation point look ordinary, because the point helped set its own scale.

questions.prompt: You run nested CV as in Listing 13.4, but with a grid of 3 × 4 = 12 combinations, a 4-fold inner `GridSearchCV` (default `refit=True`) and a 5-fold outer `cross_val_score`. How many model fits does the `cross_val_score` call perform in total? Do not count the final `search.fit(X, y)`. Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Per outer fold the inner search fits $12 \times 4 = 48$ models, then refits the winner once on the whole outer training set: 49 fits. Over 5 outer folds: $5 \times 49 = 245$. The final `search.fit(X, y)` adds another 49. Forgetting the refit gives 240, which is the most common slip.

questions.prompt: Models A and B are scored on the same 5 folds. The per-fold differences $a_i - b_i$ are $0.010, 0.004, 0.012, 0.006, 0.008$. The paired t statistic is $t = \bar d / (s_d/\sqrt{k})$, where $s_d$ is the sample std ($n-1$). What is $t$? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$\bar d = 0.040/5 = 0.008$. Deviations from the mean are $0.002, -0.004, 0.004, -0.002, 0$. Their squares sum to $40 \times 10^{-6}$, so $s_d = \sqrt{40\times10^{-6}/4} \approx 0.00316$.
$$t = \frac{0.008}{0.00316/\sqrt{5}} = \frac{0.008}{0.001414} \approx 5.66$$
The mean gap is small (0.8 points) but B loses on every fold, so the paired test finds it convincing ($p \approx 0.005$ with 4 degrees of freedom). An unpaired comparison of the two means would bury this under fold-to-fold noise.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 1,000 rows with 100 positives. Nested CV uses an outer `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5)` and, inside each outer training set, a `GridSearchCV` with `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=4)`. How many positives are in each *inner training* set? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Outer training set: 4/5 of the data, so 800 rows with 80 positives. The inner splitter cuts those 800 rows into 4 folds of 200 rows and 20 positives. Each inner training set is 3 of those folds: 600 rows with 60 positives. A tempting wrong path applies the inner fraction to the full dataset ($3/4 \times 100 = 75$). The inner loop only ever sees the outer training set.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 100 rows, 5,000 pure-noise features and random balanced labels. A script selects the 20 features most associated with `y` using `SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit_transform(X, y)` on all rows, then runs 5-fold CV of logistic regression on those 20 features. What will CV report?
options: Accuracy below 0.5, because noise features push the model to predict the opposite class
Accuracy near 0.5, because the selection step has no fitted scaler and so has nothing that could leak
Well above 0.5, because selection saw the validation labels and kept features that fit them by chance
Accuracy near 0.5, because the 5-fold rotation averages away any effect of the selection step
questions.explanation: With 5,000 noise columns, some correlate with `y` in this sample by chance. Choosing them on all rows builds that chance agreement into every validation fold. CV then rewards it. Running this in scikit-learn gives CV accuracy of about 0.80 to 0.95 across random seeds, while putting `SelectKBest` inside the `Pipeline` gives about 0.5 (0.39 to 0.59). The Pipeline rule covers *every* fitted step, not only scalers.

questions.prompt: A team runs `GridSearchCV` over 400 configurations with 5-fold CV. `best_score_` is 0.91. Nested CV with the same grid gives $0.87 \pm 0.02$. Select ALL statements that are correct.
options: Outer folds picking different hyperparameters is expected and does not invalidate the 0.87
The model to ship is the one fitted inside the best-scoring outer fold
The 0.91 is optimistic, because the same folds both chose the winner and scored it
The team should keep tuning the grid on the outer folds until both numbers agree
The honest estimate to report for this tuning procedure is about 0.87
questions.explanation: `best_score_` is the maximum over 400 CV estimates, so it carries selection bias. A large grid makes the bias larger, which is why this gap is 4 points while the book's small grid showed none. The nested score is the honest estimate. The chapter says outer folds may choose different settings and that is expected. The shipped model comes from refitting the search on all data (`search.fit(X, y)`), not from one outer fold. Tuning on outer folds would turn them into selection data and destroy the honest estimate.

questions.prompt: The one-standard-error rule picks the *simplest* model whose mean CV score is within one standard error of the best mean, where $\text{SE} = \text{fold std}/\sqrt{k}$. Ten-fold CV of a gradient-boosted model gives these mean accuracies by `max_depth`: 2 → 0.861, 3 → 0.869, 5 → 0.872, 8 → 0.874. The best model (depth 8) has a fold std of 0.019. Which depth does the rule choose? (A shallower tree counts as simpler.)
options: `max_depth=2`
`max_depth=3`
`max_depth=5`
`max_depth=8`
questions.explanation: $\text{SE} = 0.019/\sqrt{10} \approx 0.0060$. The threshold is $0.874 - 0.006 = 0.868$. Depth 3 (0.869) clears it and depth 2 (0.861) does not, so depth 3 is the simplest acceptable model. The trap is using the fold std itself as the margin: $0.874 - 0.019 = 0.855$ would admit depth 2. Picking depth 8 ignores that gaps under one SE are noise, the same point Procedure 13.5 makes.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why choosing hyperparameters based on test-set performance invalidates that test set as an estimate of generalisation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Choosing hyperparameters based on test-set performance means the model was implicitly optimised, at least in part, to do well on that exact set of examples. The test set has stopped being purely "unseen data." It has become part of the selection process. Any resulting test-set score is now measuring how well the model fits that specific set, not how well it generalises to new data.

bookExercises.prompt: State which CV strategy is correct for each: (a) a dataset of 30 rare-disease patient records; (b) daily sales figures for the past three years; (c) a roughly balanced 5,000-row classification dataset.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Leave-One-Out: 30 patient records is well under the "<50 examples" threshold for LOO. (b) TimeSeriesSplit: daily sales are strictly time-ordered, so random shuffling would leak the future into training. (c) Stratified k-fold (k=5): a roughly balanced, moderate-size dataset is the standard case Stratified k-fold with k=5 is designed for.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 13.6's pattern, compute the standard deviation of the ten seed-accuracy values (0.982, 0.991, 0.982, 0.974, 0.974, 0.982, 0.991, 0.965, 0.974, 1.000) and compare it to this chapter's 5-fold CV standard deviation (0.007). Which estimate would you trust more, and why?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The ten seed-accuracy values have a standard deviation of about 0.010 (`np.std`), roughly 1 percentage point. That's somewhat *larger* than the 5-fold CV standard deviation of 0.007. The 5-fold CV estimate is still the more trustworthy of the two, and not just because its std happens to be smaller. It's built from five disjoint folds that together cover the whole dataset exactly once, systematically. The ten single-split values, by contrast, are ten separate 80/20 splits that overlap heavily. They aren't independent measurements of the same underlying quantity, not in a structured resampling sense. A single seed's score depends entirely on which specific examples happened to land in that one test set. CV's reported score is already an average over five such sets. That's exactly why it ends up both more stable and more representative than any pile of ad hoc reshuffles, however many are tried.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 13.4, explain what it would mean if the non-nested and nested CV estimates came back nearly identical (as this chapter's own 0.9543 vs. 0.9543 result did) versus if they came back several percentage points apart.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A gap of zero, or effectively zero, between non-nested and nested estimates (like this chapter's 0.9543 vs. 0.9543 result) indicates the optimism bias is negligible for this dataset/search combination. That bias comes from selecting hyperparameters on the same data used to evaluate them. Either the dataset is easy enough to separate, or the hyperparameter search space is small enough, that overfitting to the inner CV folds isn't a serious problem here. A gap of several percentage points would indicate the opposite. The non-nested number would be meaningfully inflated by selection bias. Only the nested estimate should be reported or trusted as the honest expected performance.

bookExercises.prompt: A teammate says "I ran 5-fold CV and got 94% ± 0.5%, so I'm confident in this number." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, name one thing that CV std alone does not tell you about the estimate's reliability.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: CV std tells you how much the score varies across folds of *this* dataset with *this* model. It does not tell you whether the underlying data collection process itself is representative of the deployment population. It does not tell you whether there's target leakage baked into the features. It does not tell you whether the model will face distribution shift once deployed. A tight CV std is consistent with a reliable estimate on this data. But it says nothing about whether this data is the right data to be estimating from.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer has a time-ordered dataset but their data science team used regular `StratifiedKFold` and reported a strong result. Using this chapter's Time-Series Cross-Validation section, write the two or three sentences you'd say about why that result should not be trusted as-is.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Regular `StratifiedKFold` on time-ordered data allows validation folds that sit chronologically *before* some of the training data within the same fold rotation. That means the model may have effectively seen future information relative to what it's being scored on. The strong reported result is very likely optimistic and would not hold up once the model only has access to past data at deployment time. I'd ask them to rerun with `TimeSeriesSplit` before trusting that number."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the scikit-learn documentation's page on `cross_validate` versus `cross_val_score`. Identify one piece of information `cross_validate` returns that `cross_val_score` does not, and describe a situation from this chapter where that extra information would matter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. `cross_validate` returns fit time and score time per fold (and can return train scores alongside validation scores, and multiple metrics simultaneously) that `cross_val_score` does not. This chapter's Procedure 13.5 (comparing two models) would benefit from `cross_validate`'s per-fold timing when training cost, not just accuracy, is part of deciding between two otherwise similarly-accurate models.
